slice-method: A way of checking a slip surface: cut the soil above it into upright slices, work out the grip and the pull on each slice's base, and divide the sum of the grips by the sum of the pulls to get the factor of safety.
bishop-method: The method of slices Alan Bishop published in 1955 for circular slip surfaces. It balances each slice up and down, taking the slices' pushes on one another as horizontal, and the turning effect of the whole mass about the circle's centre. The factor of safety appears on both sides of its equation, so it is found by repeating the sum until the answer stops changing.
spencer-method: A method of slices, published by E. Spencer in 1967, that balances both the forces on the slices and their turning effects, taking the slices' pushes on one another as parallel. It works on slip surfaces of any shape, such as a block sliding along a weak layer.
pore-pressure-ratio: The share of a soil's weight that its water pressure carries, written r_u: the pore pressure at a point divided by the weight of soil above it, or for a whole slip surface the slices' Σ u·b over Σ W. 0 is dry; 0.5 means the water carries half the weight.
load-case: One set of conditions a dam's slopes are checked for, such as a full reservoir with steady seepage, the end of construction, a rapid drawdown or an earthquake. Each has its own required factor of safety.
end-of-construction: The load case of a dam just built, before the water pressure squeezed into its fill and core by the weight of the layers above has had time to drain away. New earth dams are usually asked for a factor of safety of about 1.3 in it.

entry: The surface along which a slope would slide if it failed: usually a circle for an embankment, or a broken line along a weak layer. A check tries many surfaces and keeps the one with the lowest factor of safety, the critical surface.

Lowering a reservoir faster than the water can drain out of the dam. The reservoir that pressed on the upstream face is gone, while fill and clay keep most of their water pressure, which now seeps out through the face, so that slope can slide. Free-draining rockfill lets its water go as fast as the level falls.

The part of a soil's strength that doesn't depend on how hard its grains are pressed together, written c′: on a strength line, where the line meets the axis of zero press. Clays and compacted fill have a little (the workbench gives its fill 10 kPa); clean sand and rockfill have none.
